```{webr}
#| include: false
#| autorun: true
# The specification menu, its validation, and the helpers of Tasks 4 and 5:
# try_spec(), my_experiments(), submit_exploration(), prereg(), build_model(),
# run_spec() and report_result(). Every result is read from the curve of 864
# specifications in spec_curve.csv, and every option off the curve is refused
# with the reason recorded in menu_options.csv; both files arrive through the
# `resources:` list of the including page, in the folder .data_dir. No model is
# fitted here; the IDE workspace fits the same specifications live, with their CR2
# test, and returns the same numbers.
.curve   <- utils::read.csv(file.path(.data_dir, "spec_curve.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
.options <- utils::read.csv(file.path(.data_dir, "menu_options.csv"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                            encoding = "UTF-8")
.course_url <- "https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-eu"

# The thirteen axis codes that key the curve, in its column order; the
# inference rule is the fourteenth decision and is the same for every row.
.axis_codes <- c("outcome", "predictor", "copredictor", "estimator", "sample", "weights",
                 "construction", "noop", "item_set", "cell_weight", "measure", "pred_form",
                 "family")
.neg_framings <- c("mcomm", "mlib", "mneg")

# The options that the curve keeps, in the three groups of the menu: the
# question, its measurement and the model. Every other option of the menu is
# listed in menu_options.csv.
.menu <- list(
  # The question
  my_outcome      = c("mcosmo", "mutil", "mpos"),
  my_predictor    = c("unemp", "growth"),
  my_copredictor  = c("none", "other"),
  my_estimator    = c("fe_twoway", "fe_country"),
  my_sample       = "all",
  my_weights      = "none",
  my_construction = "share",
  # Measurement
  my_noop         = c("zero", "drop"),
  my_item_set     = c("all", "un"),
  my_cell_weight  = c("unweighted", "design"),
  my_measure      = c("wb_nat", "es_1574_act", "es_2064_pop", "es_2564_lfs", "wb_growth"),
  # The model
  my_pred_form    = c("raw", "log"),
  my_family       = "gaussian",
  my_se           = "cr2"
)
.measures_for <- list(unemp  = c("wb_nat", "es_1574_act", "es_2064_pop", "es_2564_lfs"),
                      growth = "wb_growth")

if (nrow(.curve) != 864 ||
    !all(purrr::map_lgl(.axis_codes, \(a) all(.curve[[a]] %in% .menu[[paste0("my_", a)]]))))
  stop("The curve of 864 specifications did not load: reload the page.",
       call. = FALSE)
.curve_keys <- purrr::exec(paste, !!!unname(as.list(.curve[.axis_codes])), sep = "|")

.est_lab <- function(e) c(
  fe_twoway  = "two-way fixed effects (country + year)",
  fe_country = "country fixed effects")[[e]]
.se_lab <- "CR2 errors clustered by country, Satterthwaite df"

# The term for the claim-carrying predictor as it appears in a formula:
# log(unemp) when the log form is chosen, else the bare variable name.
.main_term <- function(ch) {
  if (ch$my_predictor == "unemp" && ch$my_pred_form == "log") "log(unemp)"
  else ch$my_predictor
}
.copred_term <- function(ch) if (identical(ch$my_predictor, "unemp")) "growth" else "unemp"

# --- validation ------------------------------------------------------------
# Two entry points into the same rules. .validate() takes a named list, which
# is how the exploratory try_spec() supplies its arguments; .check_choices()
# reads the fourteen my_* choices and claim_align out of the session, which is
# how the declared flow reads the preregistration cell. An option that is not
# on the curve stops with the reason from menu_options.csv, the
# workshop's page that teaches it, and the options that stay on the curve.
# A taught_on path may end in the id of a section, which the titles key and
# .page_ref() keeps in the address.
.page_titles <- c(
  "companion/measurement.qmd"      = "Scale construction",
  "companion/panel-data.qmd"       = "Panel data",
  "companion/dags.qmd"             = "Causal graphs",
  "companion/multiverse.qmd"       = "The multiverse and its critics",
  "companion/measurement.qmd#sec-noop"       = "Scale construction",
  "companion/measurement.qmd#sec-imputation" = "Scale construction",
  "companion/data-sources.qmd"     = "Social science data sources",
  "curve.qmd" = "Specification curve",
  "menu.qmd"  = "Specification menu",
  "menu.qmd#whose-average"  = "Specification menu",
  "menu.qmd#cell-weighting" = "Specification menu",
  "menu.qmd#outcome-family" = "Specification menu")
.page_ref <- function(path) {
  title <- if (path %in% names(.page_titles)) .page_titles[[path]] else path
  sprintf("%s, %s/%s", title, .course_url, sub(".qmd", ".html", path, fixed = TRUE))
}
.or_list <- function(x) {
  q <- paste0("\"", x, "\"")
  if (length(q) == 1) q else paste(paste(q[-length(q)], collapse = ", "), "or", q[length(q)])
}
# two older option codes that labels and calls may still use, mapped to the rows that hold their reasons
.legacy <- c("se:clustered" = "cr1", "weights:n_cy" = "n_cell")

.on_menu <- function(k, v) is.character(v) && length(v) == 1 && !is.na(v) && v %in% .menu[[k]]

.refuse <- function(k, v, ch, as_args) {
  shown <- function(a) if (as_args) a else paste0("my_", a)
  axis  <- sub("^my_", "", k)
  keep  <- if (k == "my_measure" && isTRUE(ch$my_predictor %in% names(.measures_for)))
    .measures_for[[ch$my_predictor]] else .menu[[k]]
  map   <- paste0("  Every decision and its options: ", .page_ref("menu.qmd"), "#map")
  if (!is.character(v) || length(v) != 1 || is.na(v))
    stop(sprintf("%s needs one option in quotes, for example %s = \"%s\".",
                 shown(axis), shown(axis), .menu[[k]][1]), call. = FALSE)
  look <- if (paste0(axis, ":", v) %in% names(.legacy)) .legacy[[paste0(axis, ":", v)]] else v
  row  <- .options[.options$axis == axis & .options$option == look & !.options$on_curve, ]
  msg <- if (nrow(row) == 1) c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" (%s) is not on the curve of 864 specifications.",
            shown(axis), v, row$label),
    paste0("  Why: ", row$reason),
    if (axis == "se")
      "  Inference is fixed: CR2 errors clustered by country, Satterthwaite df; the printout also gives the conventional t.",
    paste0("  Where it is taught: ", .page_ref(row$taught_on)),
    map,
    sprintf("  To stay on the curve, choose %s = %s.", shown(axis), .or_list(keep))
  ) else c(
    sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is not an option on the menu.", shown(axis), v),
    sprintf("  On the curve: %s.", paste(.menu[[k]], collapse = " | ")),
    if (any(.options$axis == axis & !.options$on_curve))
      sprintf("  Off the curve: %s.",
              paste(.options$option[.options$axis == axis & !.options$on_curve], collapse = " | ")),
    map
  )
  stop(paste(msg, collapse = "\n"), call. = FALSE)
}

.validate <- function(ch, as_args = FALSE) {
  shown <- function(a) if (as_args) a else paste0("my_", a)
  # the co-predictor may also be named by its variable, growth or unemp
  if (identical(ch$my_copredictor, .copred_term(ch)))
    ch <- utils::modifyList(ch, list(my_copredictor = "other"))
  bad <- purrr::discard(names(.menu), \(k) .on_menu(k, ch[[k]]))
  if (length(bad) > 0) .refuse(bad[1], ch[[bad[1]]], ch, as_args)
  if (ch$my_predictor == "growth" && ch$my_pred_form == "log")
    stop(sprintf("GDP growth takes negative values and enters raw only: use %s = \"raw\".",
                 shown("pred_form")), call. = FALSE)
  if (!ch$my_measure %in% .measures_for[[ch$my_predictor]])
    stop(sprintf("%s = \"%s\" is a series for %s; with %s = \"%s\" choose %s = %s.",
                 shown("measure"), ch$my_measure, setdiff(names(.measures_for), ch$my_predictor),
                 shown("predictor"), ch$my_predictor, shown("measure"),
                 .or_list(.measures_for[[ch$my_predictor]])), call. = FALSE)
  ch
}

.check_choices <- function() {
  need <- names(.menu)
  missing <- purrr::discard(need, \(k) exists(k))
  if (length(missing) > 0)
    stop("Not declared yet: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill in every choice of the preregistration cell and run it.",
         call. = FALSE)
  if (!exists("claim_align"))
    stop("claim_align not declared: add claim_align <- TRUE to the preregistration cell.",
         call. = FALSE)
  .validate(purrr::set_names(purrr::map(need, \(k) get(k)), need))
}

# --- the curve -------------------------------------------------------------
.key_of <- function(ch) paste(unlist(ch[paste0("my_", .axis_codes)]), collapse = "|")

.lookup <- function(ch) {
  i <- match(.key_of(ch), .curve_keys)
  if (is.na(i))
    stop("The specification passed the checks but is not among the 864 on the curve: reload the page.",
         call. = FALSE)
  .curve[i, ]
}

# One result in the form that the printout and the submission use: the
# conventional fit (b, se, t, df, r), the claim-aligned r, the CR2 test with its
# Satterthwaite df, and the placement among the 864.
.result <- function(ch) {
  hit <- .lookup(ch)
  list(b = hit$b, se = hit$se, t = hit$t, df = hit$df, n = hit$n_cells, r = hit$r,
       r_ca = hit$r_ca, p_cr2 = hit$p_cr2, df_cr2 = hit$df_cr2,
       placement = mean(.curve$r_ca < hit$r_ca),
       source = "read from the curve of 864 specifications")
}

# The claim-alignment factor. The claim expects framing to rise with growth,
# so a growth slope is reported with its sign flipped; the negative framings,
# which are not on the curve, were reverse-coded the same way. The r_ca column
# of the curve is r times this factor.
.flip <- function(ch)
  (if (ch$my_outcome %in% .neg_framings) -1 else 1) *
  (if (ch$my_predictor == "growth") -1 else 1)

# The one-line spec label that the class chart reads: six of the seven
# decisions about the question, then in brackets the scoring rule, the
# measurement decisions and the decisions about the model, with the inference
# rule last.
.spec_line <- function(ch) {
  neg <- ch$my_outcome %in% .neg_framings
  paste0(ch$my_outcome, if (neg) "_ca" else "", " ~ ", ch$my_predictor, "(", ch$my_pred_form, ")",
         if (ch$my_copredictor == "other") paste0(" + ", .copred_term(ch)) else "",
         " | ", ch$my_estimator, " | ", ch$my_sample, " | w:", ch$my_weights,
         " [", ch$my_construction, ", ", ch$my_noop, ", items:", ch$my_item_set, ", cells:",
         ch$my_cell_weight, ", ", ch$my_measure, " | ", ch$my_family, ", se:", ch$my_se, "]")
}

# four decimals, so that a p just above 0.05 never prints as 0.050
.fmt_p <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else sprintf("= %.4f", p)

.class_line <- function(res) {
  below <- res$r_ca < 0
  sig   <- res$p_cr2 < 0.05
  if (below && sig) "below zero and significant under CR2 (p < 0.05), in the direction of the claim"
  else if (below) "below zero, but not significant under CR2 (p >= 0.05)"
  else if (sig) "above zero and significant under CR2, against the direction of the claim"
  else "above zero and not significant under CR2"
}

.print_result <- function(ch, res, lead = NULL, aligned = TRUE) {
  fl <- if (aligned) .flip(ch) else 1
  writeLines(c(
    lead,
    paste0("  ", .spec_line(ch)),
    sprintf("  b = %.5f   se = %.5f   t = %.3f on %d df (conventional standard error)",
            fl * res$b, res$se, fl * res$t, round(res$df)),
    sprintf("  partial r = %.3f, %s", if (aligned) res$r_ca else res$r,
            if (aligned) "claim-aligned (below zero is the direction of the claim)"
            else "on the original scale of the outcome"),
    sprintf("  p %s with CR2 errors clustered by country, on %.1f Satterthwaite df",
            .fmt_p(res$p_cr2), res$df_cr2),
    paste0(if (aligned) "  Class: " else "  Class, on the claim-aligned scale: ", .class_line(res)),
    sprintf("  Placement: %.0f%% of the 864 specifications on the curve have a more negative claim-aligned r",
            100 * res$placement),
    if (aligned && ch$my_predictor == "growth")
      "  (growth: b, t and r with their signs flipped, since the claim expects framing to rise with growth)",
    if (!aligned)
      "  (claim_align = FALSE: shown on the original scale; the class chart receives the claim-aligned values)",
    paste0("  (", res$source, ")")))
  invisible(res)
}

# --- Task 4: the exploratory helpers ---------------------------------------
.tried <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())
assign("log", NULL, envir = .tried)
assign("last", NULL, envir = .tried)

try_spec <- function(outcome = "mcosmo", predictor = "unemp", copredictor = "none",
                     estimator = "fe_twoway", sample = "all", weights = "none",
                     construction = "share", noop = "zero", item_set = "all",
                     cell_weight = "unweighted", measure = NULL,
                     pred_form = "raw", family = "gaussian", se = "cr2") {
  if (is.null(measure)) measure <- if (identical(predictor, "growth")) "wb_growth" else "wb_nat"
  ch <- .validate(list(my_outcome = outcome, my_predictor = predictor, my_copredictor = copredictor,
                       my_estimator = estimator, my_sample = sample, my_weights = weights,
                       my_construction = construction, my_noop = noop, my_item_set = item_set,
                       my_cell_weight = cell_weight, my_measure = measure,
                       my_pred_form = pred_form, my_family = family, my_se = se), as_args = TRUE)
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, lead = "")
  fl  <- .flip(ch)
  row <- data.frame(stats::setNames(ch, sub("^my_", "", names(ch))),
                    b = fl * res$b, t = fl * res$t, r_aligned = res$r_ca, p_cr2 = res$p_cr2,
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  assign("log", purrr::list_rbind(list(.tried$log, row)), envir = .tried)
  assign("last", list(ch = ch, res = res), envir = .tried)
  invisible(row)
}

# The running log of everything try_spec() has looked up. Only the decisions
# that varied are shown; the constant ones are those of the reproduced
# specification or of every call.
my_experiments <- function() {
  d <- .tried$log
  if (is.null(d)) {
    writeLines("Nothing tried yet: call try_spec() first.")
    return(invisible(NULL))
  }
  axes   <- sub("^my_", "", names(.menu))
  varied <- names(purrr::keep(d[axes], \(x) length(unique(x)) > 1))
  show <- d |>
    datawizard::data_select(select = c(varied, "b", "t", "r_aligned", "p_cr2")) |>
    datawizard::data_modify(b = signif(b, 3), t = round(t, 2), r_aligned = round(r_aligned, 3),
                            p_cr2 = round(p_cr2, 4))
  writeLines(sprintf("Specifications tried (%d):\n", nrow(d)))
  print(show, row.names = FALSE)
  writeLines(sprintf("\nSpread of claim-aligned r: %.3f to %.3f  |  below zero and significant under CR2: %d of %d",
                     min(d$r_aligned), max(d$r_aligned),
                     sum(d$r_aligned < 0 & d$p_cr2 < 0.05), nrow(d)))
  invisible(show)
}

submit_exploration <- function(nickname = NULL) {
  if (is.null(.tried$last))
    stop("Nothing to submit: call try_spec() first; the last specification tried is the one submitted.",
         call. = FALSE)
  .submit(.tried$last$ch, .tried$last$res, "explore",
          "Exploratory submission, claim-aligned (the last specification tried):",
          nickname)
}

# --- Task 5: the declared helpers ------------------------------------------

prereg <- function() {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  writeLines(c(
    "DECLARED – the preregistered specification, fixed before it is run:",
    "",
    "  The question",
    paste("    outcome    :", ch$my_outcome),
    paste0("    predictor  : ", ch$my_predictor,
           if (ch$my_predictor == "growth") " (sign flipped to align with the claim)"),
    paste("    adjusted   :", if (ch$my_copredictor == "other") .copred_term(ch) else "nothing"),
    paste("    estimator  :", .est_lab(ch$my_estimator)),
    paste("    sample     :", ch$my_sample, "   whose average:", ch$my_weights),
    paste("    scored as  :", ch$my_construction),
    "  Measurement",
    paste("    no-opinion rule:", ch$my_noop, "  items:", ch$my_item_set),
    paste("    cells:", ch$my_cell_weight, "  series:", ch$my_measure),
    "  The model",
    paste("    form:", ch$my_pred_form, "  family:", ch$my_family, "  inference:", .se_lab),
    paste("  claim_align:", isTRUE(claim_align)),
    "",
    "build_model(), run_spec() and report_result() read these choices."))
  invisible(ch)
}

build_model <- function(formula, estimator) {
  ch <- .check_choices()
  if (missing(formula) || !inherits(formula, "formula"))
    stop("The first argument must be a formula: outcome ~ predictor terms, unquoted.",
         call. = FALSE)
  lhs <- all.vars(formula[[2]])
  if (!identical(lhs, ch$my_outcome))
    stop(sprintf("The formula has the outcome '%s'; the preregistration declares '%s'. Change the formula to match.",
                 deparse(formula[[2]]), ch$my_outcome), call. = FALSE)
  want <- c(.main_term(ch), if (ch$my_copredictor == "other") .copred_term(ch))
  got  <- attr(terms(formula), "term.labels")
  if (!setequal(got, want))
    stop(sprintf("Right-hand side { %s } does not match the preregistered { %s }.%s",
                 paste(got, collapse = ", "), paste(want, collapse = ", "),
                 if (.main_term(ch) == "log(unemp)" && !"log(unemp)" %in% got)
                   " The preregistration declares the log form: write log(unemp)." else ""),
         call. = FALSE)
  if (missing(estimator) || !identical(estimator, ch$my_estimator))
    stop(sprintf("estimator = \"%s\" does not match the preregistered \"%s\".",
                 if (missing(estimator)) "" else estimator, ch$my_estimator), call. = FALSE)
  writeLines(c("Model accepted, matching the preregistration:",
               paste0("  ", deparse(formula), ", estimated by ", .est_lab(estimator)),
               "  Run it with run_spec(my_model)."))
  structure(list(choices = ch, formula = formula, estimator = estimator), class = "spec_ticket")
}

run_spec <- function(spec) {
  if (missing(spec) || !inherits(spec, "spec_ticket"))
    stop("Pass the object that build_model() returned, e.g. run_spec(my_model).", call. = FALSE)
  now <- .check_choices()
  if (!identical(spec$choices, now))
    stop("The preregistration cell has changed since build_model(): rerun prereg() and build_model().",
         call. = FALSE)
  ch  <- spec$choices
  res <- .result(ch)
  .print_result(ch, res, "Preregistered specification, read from the curve of 864:",
                aligned = isTRUE(claim_align))
}

# Both submissions of a participant carry one short tag inside the spec label,
# "explore: [amber-otter-42] …", so that the participant can find their own
# circles on the class chart. The tag rides in the free-text label because the
# form and its fields are frozen infrastructure. The same functions sit in
# R/spec_tools.R of the IDE workspace, which keeps the tag in a file; here it lasts
# for the browser session, and a nickname passed to either submission function
# sets it or brings it back after a reload.
```

## What social science is for {#what-are-we-doing-when-we-do-social-science}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Making **claims about the world** that could turn out to be wrong – and saying how we would know.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A claim is offered to others so that they can **check it, use it, argue with it, build on it**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Science depends on that handover, and everything that follows is about whether it works.
:::
::::

::: notes
I start with a question that is seldom asked aloud, what we are doing when we do social science. [advance] We make claims about the world that could turn out to be wrong, with some statement of how we would find out. [advance] A claim is published so that other people can check it, use it, argue with it and build on it, and a finding that nobody else can examine remains an assertion. [advance] When we ask whether social science is in trouble, then, the question is quite specific: whether that handover works, and whether someone else can pick up your finding and do anything with it.
:::

## False positives and forking paths {#three-arguments-that-made-people-nervous .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **The theory, 2005.** With small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false with nobody breaking any rules [@Ioannidis2005WhyMostPublished]
- **The demonstration, 2011.** Give researchers only the flexibility they legitimately have – which cases to drop, which covariates to keep, when to stop collecting – and a **false-positive rate of 5% becomes over 60%** [@SimmonsEtAl2011FalsePositivePsychology]
- **The subtlety, 2014.** You do not need many tests. In a **garden of forking paths**, a single test *chosen after looking at the data* already has the wrong p-value [@GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience]
:::

::: notes
Three arguments made people nervous, and I take the arguments in the order of how uncomfortable they are. Ioannidis made the theoretical case in 2005: with small studies, small true effects, flexible designs and many teams chasing the same question, most published findings in a field can be false without anybody breaking a rule. Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn then demonstrated it, showing that the flexibility which researchers legitimately have can push a false-positive rate of five per cent above sixty, and they made the point by 'showing', with real participants and real statistics, that listening to a Beatles song makes people younger. Gelman and Loken added the point that I find hardest to set aside: no long series of tests is needed, since a single test chosen after looking at the data already has the wrong p-value.
:::

## Evidence from replications and many-analysts studies {#and-then-people-counted .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **100 psychology studies**, replicated with high power and the original materials: **97%** of the originals were significant, **36%** of the replications were, and effect sizes roughly **halved** [@OpenScienceCollaboration2015EstimatingReproducibilityPsychological]
- **161 researchers, 73 teams, one hypothesis** on immigration and support for social policy: **1,253** models, and no convergence on either sign or significance [@BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Different fields and different designs. In the first, **most findings were not significant again in new samples**; in the second, **the result depended on who ran the analysis.**
:::

::: notes
Then people counted. The Open Science Collaboration replicated a hundred psychology studies with high power and the original materials. Ninety-seven per cent of the original studies had reported a significant result, thirty-six per cent of the replications did, and the effect sizes came back at about half their original size, and this is the study that carried the phrase 'replication crisis' outside methods seminars. The second study is closer to our own fields: seventy-three teams, one hypothesis about immigration and support for social policy, more than twelve hundred models between them, and no agreement on the sign, let alone the significance. [advance] In the first study most findings were not significant again in new samples, while in the second the result depended on who ran the analysis.
:::

## Incentives and questionable research practices {#it-is-not-mostly-fraud .smaller}

::: {.small}
Fraud exists, but it is rare. The mechanism behind these results is **ordinary and structural**:

- Journals reward novel, clean, significant results – so that is what gets written up
- Every analysis contains dozens of small defensible choices, and the analyst makes them while looking at the data
- Nobody publishes the twelve specifications that did not work; the reader sees one
- Data and code are usually not available, so nobody can check any of it
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Ask researchers anonymously, with an incentive to answer truthfully, and a **majority admit** to at least one of these ordinary practices [@JohnEtAl2012MeasuringPrevalenceQuestionable]
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
None of these steps requires a dishonest person, so the problem cannot be fixed by hiring better people.
:::

::: notes
This is not mostly a story about fraud, which is rare and is not what these numbers measure. The mechanism is ordinary and structural. Journals want novel, clean, significant results, so that is what gets submitted. Every analysis contains dozens of small choices, each defensible on its own, which the analyst makes while looking at the data. Nobody writes up the twelve specifications that did not work, so the reader meets one path through a garden of hundreds, and the data and the code are usually unavailable, so nobody can check. [advance] John, Loewenstein and Prelec asked researchers anonymously, with a mechanism that made truthful answers worth giving, and a majority admitted to at least one of these practices. [advance] None of these steps requires a bad actor, so the problem cannot be solved by hiring better people. [pause] Suppose, then, that we gave the best people we could find the same data and the same question, and recorded what they did.
:::

## The red-card study {#twenty-nine-teams-one-question .smaller}

::: {.small}
**The question.** Are football referees more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones?

**The data.** One dataset, sent to everyone: 2,053 players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the 3,147 referees they played under, and **146,028 player–referee pairs**. Skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who did not know the research question.

**The design.** Twenty-nine teams analysed it independently. They reviewed each other's approaches *before* anyone had seen a result, revised, and only then compared answers.
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
This is the first many-analysts study. Every one since is a variation on it, including the one that this workshop works on.
:::

::: {.src}
@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne
:::

::: notes
Silberzahn and colleagues ran very nearly that experiment, in a study published in 2018, and every many-analysts study since, the one in which I took part included, varies its design. The question was whether football referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players than to light-skinned ones. Everyone received the same data: two thousand and fifty-three players in the top divisions of England, Germany, France and Spain, the more than three thousand referees under whom they had played, and a hundred and forty-six thousand player–referee pairs, with skin tone rated from profile photographs by two coders who were not told the research question. Twenty-nine teams analysed the data independently, reviewed each other's approaches before anybody had a result, revised, and only then compared answers, so that nobody could tune a method towards a number that they liked.
:::

## 'Replication' crises

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Another 'replication' crisis – terminological confusion?
:::
::: {.fragment}
The term 'reproducibility' has been used as a synonym for a number of different characteristics – reproducibility, robustness, replicability, repeatability, credibility, and trustworthiness [@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms, p. 2].
:::
[[Successfully rerun the same code on the same data?]{colour="#b22222"}]{.fragment}
[[Re-analyse the same data a different way?]{colour="#1C69A8"}]{.fragment}
[[Collect fresh data and analyse it in the same way?]{colour="#4D179A"}]{.fragment}
[[Using the same data and same analysis but asking a different question?]{colour="#3C6301"}]{.fragment}
[[Asking the same question but answering it with fresh data and a different analysis?]{colour="#3BB8DB"}]{.fragment}
::::

::: notes
Twenty-nine competent teams worked on one dataset and did not agree, and I have not yet said what kind of failure that is. Part of the difficulty lies in the word. [advance] For years 'replication' covered rerunning someone's code, reanalysing their data in a different way and collecting new data altogether, three operations that answer three different questions. Because all three were called 'replication', the debates about the crisis had people talking past each other for a decade, so before any more numbers we need the vocabulary. [advance through the five questions]
:::

::: notes
The grid holds that vocabulary, and if you take one thing home, I would like it to be this grid. The question stays the same in every cell, while the data and the analysis vary. Reproducibility is the same data under the same analysis, and it asks whether rerunning the recipe gives the same number. Robustness keeps the data and replaces the analysis with another justifiable one, and asks whether the finding survives defensible choices made by someone else. Replicability applies the same analysis to new data. The fourth cell, new data under a new analysis, is generalisability, which we leave aside. Everything that follows refers back to this grid.
:::

## Repeatability and credibility {#credibility-is-not-truth}

::: {.scaled style="--fs: 0.85; --lh: 1.15"}
"**Repeatability** is used when referring to reproducibility, robustness, and replicability as a constellation of concepts intended to assess whether answers to scientific questions are unchanged when different steps of the research process are repeated."

**Credibility** and **trustworthiness** refer to the confidence one can have in research findings. Because scientific knowledge claims are tentative, they are *not* synonymous with truth.

"For example, credibility is advanced by addressing potential competing interests in the conducting and reporting of research, by taking existing knowledge into account, by using methods that have been validated, by controlling for biases in the research context, by pursuing precise and reliable evidence, and by calibrating the strength of the claims to the uncertainty of the evidence."
:::

::: {.src}
@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms [p. 2]
:::

::: notes
The glossary separates two things that we routinely run together. Repeatability is the umbrella term, reproducibility, robustness and replicability taken as a family, all asking whether the answer survives the repetition of some step of the research process. Credibility and trustworthiness concern how much confidence a finding deserves, and the sentence in the middle of the slide says that, because scientific claims are tentative, credibility is not the same as truth, so a credible finding can be wrong. Credibility is built from the list at the bottom: declared interests, validated methods, precise evidence, and claims calibrated to the uncertainty behind them, the last of which recurs throughout the day.
:::

- 'Reviewer 3' takes a special interest because he's just working on a similar paper on data they published recently. Do your results [replicate]{.fragment .bounceIn} when your methods are applied to that state-of-the-art dataset?

## Open research: the practices {.smaller}

::: {.small}
| Practice | What it makes possible |
|---|---|
| **Open data** | Someone else can re-analyse your evidence |
| **Open code** | Someone else can rerun your exact analysis |
| **Open materials** | Someone else can run your study again |
| **Open access** | Someone else can read the claim in the first place |
| **Preregistration** | A dated record of the analysis plan, filed in a registry before the results exist |
| **Registered reports** | Peer review of the plan, with publication decided before results |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Each one removes a specific obstacle, and none of them guards against every problem. The programme, set out at length: [@MunafoEtAl2017ManifestoReproducibleScience]
:::

::: notes
Each of those reviewers needed something from you before they could start, your code, your data or your materials, and open research is a list of practices that supply them, each removing one identifiable obstacle. Open data lets someone else reanalyse your evidence, open code lets them rerun your exact analysis, and open materials let them run the study again in a new sample. Open access lets them read the paper at all, which sounds trivial until you try to obtain a paper from outside a wealthy university. Preregistration produces a dated record of the analysis plan, filed before the results exist, and registered reports go further, since the plan is peer-reviewed and the decision to publish is taken before anyone has a result. [advance] None of these practices guards against every problem, and whether published findings hold up when somebody checks them has now been measured on a large scale.
:::

## Confounders, mediators and colliders {#dag-crash-course-three-roles .smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](day_files/figure-revealjs/mini-dags-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.src}
X = predictor, Y = outcome. **Green** = the causal effect you want; **coloured** = the path you must reason about.
:::

::: notes
The causal graph serves the second of those steps, and these three small graphs cover all the theory of graphs that the tasks need. In every panel the green arrow is the effect of X on Y that you are after, and what changes is the coloured structure around it. A confounder is a common cause of predictor and outcome, and its red fork is a back-door path, which biases the estimate while it stays open, so you adjust for the confounder to close it. A mediator lies on the causal path between the two, and since the amber path is part of the total effect, you do not adjust for the mediator if the total effect is what you want. A collider is caused by both sides, and its edges are harmless until you condition on it, which opens a spurious path. The rules are short: adjust for confounders, leave mediators alone for a total effect, and never condition on a collider.
:::

## Reading a DAG: open and closed paths {.smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](day_files/figure-revealjs/backdoor-paths-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
Association flows along **every open path**, not only along the causal arrow. A fork or a chain is open until you adjust for the variable in its middle. A collider is the reverse: shut by default, and opened when you adjust for it.

- **Back-door criterion**: close every path that enters X from behind, keep the causal X → Y path open
- Only an adjustment set that does this supports a causal reading
:::

::: {.src}
@HernanRobins2020CausalInferenceWhat; @Huntington-Klein2021EffectIntroductionResearch.
:::

::: notes
A DAG is read through its paths. Association flows along every open path between X and Y, not only along the causal arrow, so the job is to work out which paths are open and to close the ones that you do not want. Two rules do all the work. A path through a fork or a chain is open, and you close it by adjusting for the variable in the middle, as with the red back-door fork on the left, whereas a path through a collider is closed by default and opened by adjustment. The back-door criterion combines the two rules: close every path that enters X from behind, and leave the causal path from X to Y open. Only an adjustment set that does this supports a causal reading of the estimate.
:::

## Total effect or direct effect {#which-effect-do-you-even-want .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}


::: {.cell}

:::
:::


:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.small}
- **Total** = direct (green) + indirect (amber)
- Adjust for the mediator M → you estimate the **direct** effect only – a *different* estimand
- 'Control for everything' can switch you to an estimand you never chose
- **Table 2 fallacy**: the other coefficients in your model are *not* all causal effects
:::
:::
::::

::: {.src}
@KeeleEtAl2020CausalInterpretationEstimated; @DAgostinoMcGowanEtAl2024CausalInferenceNot.
:::

::: notes
Suppose that M lies between your predictor and your outcome. The total effect is the green arrow plus the amber route through M, and the direct effect is the green arrow alone. These are different numbers answering different questions, and which one you obtain depends on whether M is in the model, so that a mediator added as one more 'control' switches the estimate to the direct effect without anyone noticing, the analyst included. This is why 'control for everything' is poor advice. A corollary is the Table 2 fallacy: in a printed regression table usually only one coefficient has a clean causal reading, and the coefficients of the control variables are not causal effects of their own.
:::

## Selection and feedback {#spurious-by-design-selection-feedback .smaller}


::: {.cell}

::: {.small}
- **Selection / collider bias** – conditioning, or merely *sampling*, on a common effect manufactures an association that was never there (much of the early COVID risk-factor literature)
- **Reverse causation & feedback** – in a panel, today's outcome can move tomorrow's predictor; two-way fixed effects absorb stable country traits and common-year shocks, **not** time-varying feedback (U = unemployment, F = framing)

::: {.src}
@GriffithEtAl2020ColliderBiasUndermines; @ColeEtAl2010IllustratingBiasDue; @LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse.

::: notes
Two last ways in which a relationship can be spurious both apply to our case study. The first is selection, or collider bias: conditioning on, or merely sampling on, something that both variables cause produces a correlation out of nothing, as in much of the early research on risk factors for COVID, which drew on people who had been tested, a selected group. The second is reverse causation and feedback. Our data are a panel, in which today's outcome can feed tomorrow's predictor. Two-way fixed effects, the baseline design for our claim, absorb stable differences between countries and shocks common to a year, but they do not on their own deal with a time-varying confounder or a feedback loop, which matters when we build the graph for our own paper.
:::

## Few clusters and the CR2 test {#few-clusters-and-the-cr2-test .smaller}

::: {.small}
| Test | Two-way fixed effects (C6HJR) | Country fixed effects, on the country-year panel |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Conventional | t = −3.80 on 233 df, p = 0.0002 | t = −6.87 on 242 df |
| Clustered by country, CR1 | t = −2.31 on 26 df, p = 0.029 | t = −3.62 on 26 df |
| Clustered, CR2, Satterthwaite df | t = −2.23 on 9.8 df, p = 0.0504 | t = −3.51 on 8.5 df, p = 0.0072 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The estimate is the same in every row; only the test changes. The years of one country are not independent, 27 countries are few clusters of unequal weight, and the CR2 test with Satterthwaite df, which classes every point of the curve, counts the countries that effectively carry the evidence.
:::

::: notes
All three reproduced t-values treat each row as independent evidence, although the years of one country resemble each other. Clustering by country allows any pattern of correlation within a country, and the evidence then rests on twenty-seven countries rather than two hundred and seventy rows. With so few clusters, of very unequal weight, the usual clustered test is still too generous, so the workshop uses the CR2 correction, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, which count how many countries effectively carry the information, fewer than ten here. In my row, the same estimate goes from a p of two in ten thousand to just above point zero five, while the design of KQXUE, fitted on the country-year panel, stays significant under every test. ## Building a scale – mean, sum or share {#building-a-scale-mean-sum-or-share .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

:::: {.columns}

## The copredictor {#copredictor-control-or-second-exposure .smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
Put GDP growth in beside unemployment and you have made a choice you should be able to name:

- **As a confounder** – a slump raises unemployment *and* sours sentiment in the same year. Adjusting closes a back-door path that your fixed effects leave open
- **As a rival exposure** – growth is a second measure of the same "poor economic performance". Now you are asking which of the two the claim is about
- **As a mediator** – if unemployment works *through* growth, adjusting removes part of the effect you wanted
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The line of code is the same in all three cases, but each reading of it targets a different estimand. And remember the **Table 2 fallacy**, which is to read every coefficient in a regression table as a causal effect. The growth coefficient in that model is not automatically the causal effect of growth.
:::

::: notes
The copredictor looks like one of the most innocuous choices on the menu, and it is easy to get wrong, because adding GDP growth beside unemployment is a choice that you should be able to name. As a confounder, growth stands for a slump that raises unemployment and sours sentiment in the same year, and adjusting for it closes a back-door path that fixed effects cannot reach. As a rival exposure, it is another measure of poor economic performance, and you are asking which of the two the claim is about. As a mediator, if unemployment works partly through growth, adjusting for it removes part of the effect that you set out to measure. ## Making the axes comparable {.smaller .deepdive run="methods"}

::: {.small}
A coefficient on a share and one on a count, or one from a model of country-years and one from a model of respondents, are not on the same scale. The robustness study and this workshop put them on one scale in three steps:

- Take the test statistic and the degrees of freedom of its fit
- Convert to a **partial correlation** *r* – the association between predictor and outcome, net of everything else in the model, on a fixed −1 to +1 scale
- Apply **claim alignment**, so the sign means the same thing everywhere
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The df must count the units that carry the evidence. Fed the clustered *t* of the reproduced specification on 26 df, the formula returns *r* = −0.413 in place of −0.242 with the estimate unchanged, so the curve, and every class submission, takes its height from the conventional fit and its class from the CR2 test.
:::

::: notes

## Where the idea comes from {.smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.skiplink}
[Multiverse tutorial, 8 slides – skip to the class chart →](#the-class-multiverse)
:::

::: {.small}
- **Multiverse analysis** [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse] – developed for *data-processing* choices: how you code, exclude and combine. Report the whole set of datasets that your choices could have produced
- **Specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis] – the same move for *model* choices, plus a visual grammar: estimates on top, the choices that produced each one underneath
- **The vibration of effects** – the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology
- **The book-length treatment** [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational] – computational recipes at scale
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Under all these names the proposal is the same: **stop treating your analytical choices as invisible, and enumerate them.**
:::

::: notes
The vocabulary of this field is confused, so I take the terms in the order in which they arrived. Multiverse analysis comes from Steegen and colleagues in 2016 and grew out of the choices of data processing, how a variable is coded, which cases are excluded and how items are combined, with the proposal to report the whole set of datasets that those choices could have produced. Specification curve analysis, by Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, makes the same move for the choices of the model and adds a display, with the estimates on top and, beneath them, a panel of the choices that produced each one. The vibration of effects is the same idea, arrived at independently in epidemiology, and there is now a book-length treatment with computational recipes. [advance] Under all these names the proposal is to stop treating analytical choices as invisible and to enumerate them.
:::

## Filters for inclusion {#justifiable-not-merely-possible .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Two filters decide which of the analyses you could run go into a multiverse:

- **Justifiability** – could you defend this specification to a reviewer, in writing, before seeing its result?
- **The same estimand** – does it estimate the quantity you said you were after?
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Drop the first filter and you get a cloud of nonsense that makes any finding look fragile. Drop the second and you are averaging over answers to different questions – which is the red-card mistake, at scale.
:::

## Enumeration and curation {#enumerate-or-curate .smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**Enumerate**

Cross every option on every axis. Complete, mechanical, reproducible.

Risk: the set fills up with specifications that nobody would defend, and the spread stops meaning anything.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}

Include only the specifications you would actually defend.

::: notes
There are two strategies for building the set, and both have a real cost. To enumerate is to cross every option on every axis mechanically, which is complete and reproducible and protects you from the charge of hand-picking, but the set then fills with specifications that nobody would defend, and once it does, the spread stops meaning anything, since analyses that are wrong were included. To curate is to include only the specifications that you would defend in print, which solves the first problem and creates a second, because you now choose the set, and a sceptic can reasonably ask whether you chose it to produce the picture that you wanted. I do not think that this dilemma can be escaped. [advance] Either way the set is a claim, which belongs in the paper beside the curve and is ideally preregistered before the curve is drawn.

## Reading a specification curve {.smaller .deepdive run="multiverse"}

::: {.small}
Five questions to ask any curve you meet, in any paper:

1. **What is on the vertical axis** – a raw coefficient, or something standardised? Are the signs aligned so that up and down mean the same thing throughout?
2. **How was the set built** – enumerated or curated, and by whom?
3. **Where does the published estimate sit** – at the median, or out at an end?
4. **Is the spread patterned** – does one axis produce the extremes, or is it scattered?
5. **What test classes the points, and against what null** – are the errors clustered, and are the specifications independent? (They almost never are.)
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Answered for your own curve, the five make a publishable robustness section.
:::

::: notes
The tutorial closes with five questions to ask of any specification curve, in anybody's paper. The first is what the vertical axis shows, a raw coefficient, which is not comparable across outcomes, or something standardised, and whether the signs are aligned so that up and down mean the same thing throughout. The second is how the set was built, enumerated or curated, and by whom, and the third where the published estimate sits, at the median or at one end, two very different situations for an author. The fourth is whether the spread is patterned, with one axis producing the extremes, or scattered. The fifth, which few people ask, is which test classes the points, against what null, with or without errors that allow for clustering, and whether the specifications are independent of each other, which they almost never are. [advance] Answered for your own curve, the five questions give the material for a publishable section on robustness.

## The permutation design {#building-the-nothing-the-permutation-design}

::: {.small}
- Break the one link that the claim needs: **shuffle each country's unemployment series in time** (jointly with growth), keeping everything else intact
- Refit **every specification on the curve** on each shuffled dataset, and repeat **B = 500** times
- Compare the observed curve to the 500 null curves: is ours more extreme than chance produces?
:::

::: {.src}
The design is worked through in your inference reading; permutation inference after @PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues.
:::

::: notes
The claim says that the unemployment of a country moves its EU framing over time. To build the null, the unemployment series of each country is shuffled in time, together with growth, so that the macro side stays internally coherent, while the framing data stay untouched. In a shuffled panel the alignment between unemployment and framing is broken by construction, so any curve obtained from it is what chance alone produces on these data with these specifications. Done five hundred times, with the entire curve refitted each time, this gives five hundred null curves against which to compare ours. If our curve falls in the far tail of those null curves, the curve as a whole is evidence, and if it falls comfortably among them, the description stands and the inference does not.
:::

## Reading a curve-level test {#how-to-read-a-curve-level-test .smaller}

::: {.small}
- With B = 500, the smallest reportable p is **2/(B+1) ≈ 0.004**, a floor set by the number of draws, not a zero
- Near p = .05 the Monte-Carlo error is about **±0.01**, so treat p = .04 and p = .06 as the same finding
- [A DESIGN, NOT YET RUN]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – a curve-level test has to be fully specified before anyone runs it, and this one has not been run; today we read the design only
:::

::: notes

Near point zero five the Monte Carlo error is around plus or minus point zero one, so a permutation p of point zero four and one of point zero six count as the same finding. ## Two points from the literature {#two-sentences-worth-keeping}

::: {.claimcard}
"the common single-path analyses in social and behavioural research should not be simply assumed to be robust to alternative analyses" [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness]
:::

::: {.claimcard}
A blueprint: precise question → causal reasoning (DAG) → multiverse → sensitivity analysis [@AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial]
:::

::: {.small}
- Same-conclusion robustness and same-*number* robustness are different bars
- Justifiability is the criterion – choose with reasons, show the spread
:::

::: notes
The first point comes from the article on the robustness study, that single-path analyses should not simply be assumed to be robust. Today the preregistration protected your choice from being opportunistic, but it gave your declared dot no special status within the curve, since the declared path is still one path among eight hundred and sixty-four, so a report needs the declared path and the space around it together. From Auspurg and Brüderl comes the constructive sequence that we followed: a precise question, explicit assumptions, the multiverse and the analysis of sensitivity. Keep the two standards of robustness apart in your own writing, the same conclusion, reached by seventy-four per cent of the reanalyses in the robustness study, and the same number, reached by thirty-four, and say which one you mean when you claim robustness.
:::
